Predictive-biomarker research offers a useful analogy: evaluate whether a diagnostic selects the better intervention, rather than merely correlating with baseline performance. Biomarker-stratified designs assess treatment-effect dependence on the marker; strategy designs evaluate the resulting selection policy. Applied here, a feasible prospective pilot would preregister diagnostic definitions, thresholds, intervention mapping, fallback behavior, compute budgets, and paired comparisons against both always-baseline and always-intervention policies before observing intervention outcomes. This is a proposed adaptation, not an established four-dataset protocol. [Freidlin et al.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2911042/)

Repeatedly choosing interventions or thresholds using the same validation HR@10 can overfit the selection criterion; reported validation gains then cannot independently establish diagnostic predictive value. Freeze the policy before new comparisons, retain all four categories, and report category-specific intervention gains alongside macro-average policy gains over both controls. Existing results used to develop the rule remain exploratory. If independent evaluation is unavailable during search, characterize the exercise as a preregistered validation pilot, with confirmation deferred to the host’s untouched final evaluation. [Cawley and Talbot](https://jmlr.csail.mit.edu/beta/papers/v11/cawley10a.html)

Four categories sharply limit inference about generalization across datasets; benchmarking research likewise warns of low power with few datasets. For a conventional exact paired sign-flip test, assuming independent categories and valid sign exchangeability, four nonzero differences yield only 16 assignments: the smallest attainable one-sided p-value is 0.0625, and the usual two-sided minimum is 0.125. These bounds follow by enumeration. Users, seeds, and checkpoints do not create additional independent categories. Emphasize effect sizes, consistency, failures, and descriptive diagnostic–gain alignment rather than claims of statistical confirmation. [Bouthillier et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.03098)
